def: An authentication layer for online card payments that can verify the cardholder with their bank.
A service that refreshes stored card details when cards are reissued, reducing failed recurring payments.
The US bank-to-bank network used for eChecks, direct debits and many recurring payments. Typically cheaper than cards but slower to settle.
The bank that holds the merchant's account and receives card payments on the merchant's behalf.
A check that compares the billing address a customer enters with the address on file at the card issuer — a key fraud tool for online and phone orders.
Fees charged by the card networks on transactions, separate from interchange and the processor's markup.
The real-time request to the card issuer to approve a transaction and hold the funds.
A group of authorized transactions sent together for settlement, usually at the end of the business day.
A transaction where the card isn't physically presented — online, phone or mail orders. CNP usually carries higher interchange and fraud risk.
A transaction where the card is dipped, tapped or swiped at a terminal.
A pricing approach that offers a lower price for cash payments. Program rules and disclosures vary by card network and state.
A disputed transaction reversed by the cardholder's bank, often with a fee to the merchant.
A fee for using an alternative payment channel (for example paying online instead of in person). Card-network rules restrict when it can be charged.
The security code printed on a card, used to verify card-not-present transactions.
Displaying both a cash price and a card price so card processing cost is covered at checkout — the basis of MCCPS Zero Processing Fees.
A fee some processors charge for ending a contract before its term ends.
Total processing fees divided by total card volume — the clearest single measure of what accepting cards costs you.
The chip-card standard. EMV transactions are more secure than magstripe swipes and affect who bears counterfeit-fraud liability.
One blended percentage (and often a per-transaction fee) for every transaction regardless of card type.
When a cardholder disputes a legitimate purchase — for example, forgetting a charge or a family member's purchase.
Software that securely transmits online and card-not-present payment data to the processor.
The fee paid to the card-issuing bank on each transaction, set by the card networks. It's the largest part of processing cost and varies by card type and how the card is accepted.
A pricing model that passes interchange and assessments through at cost and adds a disclosed processor markup.
An individual who refers or signs merchants for a processor or ISO, typically earning residuals.
A company registered with card networks through a sponsor bank to sell and support merchant accounts.
The bank that issued the customer's card and approves or declines transactions.
Additional transaction details (tax amount, PO number, line items) that can qualify business and purchasing cards for lower interchange.
A database of merchants whose accounts were terminated for certain reasons, which other acquirers check during approval.
A bank account that lets a business accept card payments and receive settled funds.
The monthly report from your processor showing volume, transactions and every fee charged.
Tiered-pricing buckets for transactions that don't meet the processor's 'qualified' criteria — they cost more.
Settlement that deposits funds the business day after a batch is closed.
Near-field communication — the technology behind tap-to-pay cards and mobile wallets.
Point-to-point encryption: card data is encrypted at the terminal and only decrypted by the processor.
A provider that signs merchants up under its own master merchant account, rather than giving each a dedicated account.
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — security requirements for any business that accepts card payments.
A monthly fee some processors charge until a merchant completes PCI validation.
Holding an amount on a card before the final total is known — common at bars, hotels and fuel pumps.
The processor's own margin on top of interchange and assessments — the negotiable part of your cost.
Automatically charging customers on a schedule for subscriptions, memberships or plans.
The merchant's response to a chargeback, submitting evidence to reverse it.
Funds a processor holds back from settlements to cover potential chargebacks or risk.
Ongoing payments to sales agents based on the processing volume of merchants they signed.
The process of moving funds from issuing banks to the merchant's account after a batch is submitted.
An added fee on credit card transactions to offset processing costs. Subject to card-network rules, disclosure requirements and state law.
A rental agreement for card hardware — often long-term and non-cancellable.
A pricing model that groups transactions into qualified, mid-qualified and non-qualified rates.
Replacing card numbers with tokens so sensitive data isn't stored in your systems.
A browser-based tool for keying in card payments taken by phone or mail.
MCCPS's compliant dual-pricing program that can take card processing cost to $0.
